articles.title: A Harnessed LLM Agent Is More Than Four Circles
articles.excerpt: Why a Runtime-Centric Architecture Is a Stronger Model for Agent Engineering A reply to The Harness Behind Reliable LLM Agents, the post that introduced the diagram A Harnessed LLM Agent. The diagram…
articles.body: Why a Runtime-Centric Architecture Is a Stronger Model for Agent Engineering A reply to The Harness Behind Reliable LLM Agents , the post that introduced the diagram A Harnessed LLM Agent . The diagram A Harnessed LLM Agent makes an important point: a capable agent is more than an LLM connected to a collection of tools. It needs reusable skills, memory, interaction protocols, execution controls, and mechanisms for evaluating its behavior. That is a useful conceptual overview. But a conceptual overview is not automatically a sound reference architecture. The diagram presents four ideas— Skills, Harness, Memory, and Protocols —as its main categories. The problem is that these ideas describe different architectural dimensions.

articles.body: Scheduled broken-link and redirect checks that tell you the moment a link breaks — linkbruno.com Open any mature codebase and search for stackoverflow.com . You'll find a few dozen comments like this: // Safari doesn't fire 'change' on autofill, see // https://stackoverflow.com/a/<answer-id> Some teams love these. Some ban them in code review. Most have never discussed it. I think it's worth arguing about, because the answer affects how future maintainers understand the strangest parts of your code. The case for linking It explains the why in one line. The hardest code to maintain is a workaround with no explanation. Why is there a setTimeout(fn, 0) here? Why is this header set twice?

articles.title: Why red ink vanishes under a red sheet, and how I made an iPhone do it
articles.excerpt: I work on Red Sheet at W Lab. Students in Japan write answers in red or orange pen, lay a sheet of red plastic over the page, and the answers disappear while the black questions stay. Slide the sheet…
articles.body: I work on Red Sheet at W Lab. Students in Japan write answers in red or orange pen, lay a sheet of red plastic over the page, and the answers disappear while the black questions stay. Slide the sheet down and you check yourself one line at a time. Red Sheet is an iPhone and iPad app that does this to a photo of your own notebook. This post is about the engine that finds the ink and hides it. Why the paper trick works, and why a filter isn't enough Red plastic passes red light and blocks the rest. Through it, white paper looks red and red ink looks red, so the ink has nothing to stand out against. Black ink reflects no red either way, so it stays dark. Green highlighter is the opposite case: it reflects almost no red, so through the sheet it turns nearly black and blocks the word under it.

articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.title: 'Arrival' at 10: Denis Villeneuve's alien visitation classic that reminded us it's good to talk
articles.excerpt: How the 'Dune' director turned a little-known short story into one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century
articles.body: In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication. But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.

articles.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
